claim: In systemic light chain amyloidosis, an overexpressed antibody light chain (LC) forms fibrils which deposit in organs and cause their failure.
source: In systemic light chain amyloidosis, an overexpressed antibody light chain (LC) forms fibrils which deposit in organs and cause their failure.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by general scientific knowledge about AL amyloidosis.

claim: Mutations in the LC's VL domain are important prerequisites for amyloidogenesis.
source: While it is well-established that mutations in the LC's VL domain are important prerequisites, the mechanisms which render a patient LC amyloidogenic are ill-defined.
evidence: The manuscript states this is well-established, indicating it is supported by existing scientific knowledge.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of the patient LC resulting in an isolated VL domain is essential for fibril formation.
source: We show that proteolytic cleavage of the patient LC resulting in an isolated VL domain is essential for fibril formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically fibril formation assays and patient tissue analysis.

claim: Out of 11 mutations in the patient VL, only one, a leucine to valine mutation, is responsible for fibril formation.
source: Out of 11 mutations in the patient VL, only one, a leucine to valine mutation, is responsible for fibril formation.
evidence: This is supported by systematic mutagenesis experiments and fibril formation assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The leucine to valine mutation disrupts a hydrophobic network rendering the C-terminal segment of VL more dynamic and decreasing domain stability.
source: It disrupts a hydrophobic network rendering the C-terminal segment of VL more dynamic and decreasing domain stability.
evidence: This is supported by H/DX-MS data, crystal structure analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: AL amyloidosis is the most common form of systemic amyloidosis.
source: Amyloid light chain (AL) amyloidosis is the most common form of systemic amyloidosis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of amyloidosis.

claim: AL amyloidosis results from an anomalous monoclonal plasma B cell proliferation in the bone marrow which leads to overproduction of immunoglobulin light chains.
source: It is the result of an anomalous monoclonal plasma B cell proliferation in the bone marrow which leads to a subsequent overproduction of immunoglobulin light chains (LC) (Baden et al., 2009; Gertz, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Normally, immunoglobulins are secreted as disulfide-bonded complexes comprising two heavy chains and two light chains.
source: Normally, immunoglobulins (Igs) are secreted as disulfide-bonded complexes comprising two heavy chains (HCs) and two LCs (Baden et al., 2008; Feige et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: In AL patients, free LCs excessively escape cellular protein quality control and are secreted into the blood stream.
source: In AL patients, free LCs excessively escape cellular protein quality control and are secreted into the blood stream.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Amyloid precursor LCs can be taken up by cells or deposit extracellularly in organs or tissues.
source: From there, the amyloid precursor LCs can be taken up by cells or deposit extracellularly in organs or tissues (Baden et al., 2008; Falk et al., 1997; Feige et al., 2010; Gertz, 2016; Kastritis and Dimopoulos, 2016; Marin-Argany et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: LCs are composed of an N-terminal variable (VL) and a constant domain (CL).
source: The LCs are composed of an N-terminal variable (VL) and a constant domain (CL).
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibody structure.

claim: The VL sequence is the result of DNA rearrangements involving a variable (V), a diversity (D) and a joining (J) gene segment.
source: The VL sequence is the result of DNA rearrangements involving a variable (V), a diversity (D) and a joining (J) gene segment (Bernard et al., 1978; Hozumi and Tonegawa, 1976; Maki et al., 1980; Tonegawa, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational research on antibody gene rearrangement.

claim: Directed hypermutation of the V region exon further increases the natural diversity of VL domains.
source: At later stages of differentiation, directed hypermutation of the V region exon further increases the natural diversity of VL domains (Feige et al., 2010; Jung and Alt, 2004; Li et al., 2004; Wilson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on somatic hypermutation.

claim: Each AL amyloidosis patient possesses a different set of somatic mutations and hence a unique disease-responsible LC sequence.
source: As a result, each AL amyloidosis patient possesses a different set of somatic mutations and hence a unique disease-responsible LC sequence (Blancas-Mejía et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations often destabilize patient LCs compared to non-amyloidogenic LCs.
source: These mutations often destabilize patient LCs compared to non-amyloidogenic LCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The destabilization of patient LCs was linked to amyloid fibril formation propensity.
source: The destabilization was linked to amyloid fibril formation propensity (Baden et al., 2008; Blancas-Mejía et al., 2015; Hurle et al., 1994; Raffen et al., 1999; Ramirez-Alvarado, 2012; Wall et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Patient biopsies predominantly revealed VL domains that result from proteolytic cleavage of the LC as the main constituent of amyloid deposits.
source: Even though full length LCs and other proteins have recently been found as part of fibrils, patient biopsies predominantly revealed VL domains that result from proteolytic cleavage of the LC as the main constituent of amyloid deposits (Blancas-Mejía et al., 2015; Buxbaum, 1986; Enqvist et al., 2009; Gallo et al., 1996; Glenner et al., 1970; Hurle et al., 1994; Nokwe et al., 2014; Pepys, 2006; Simpson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Partial unfolding of the pathogenic VLs leads to exposed residue segments that entail the stacking capability of the domain, leading to the tightly packed, dehydrated cross-β amyloid fibril structure.
source: Partial unfolding of the pathogenic VLs leads to exposed residue segments that entail the stacking capability of the domain, leading to the tightly packed, dehydrated cross-β amyloid fibril structure (Annamalai et al., 2016; Brumshtein et al., 2018; Kelly, 1998; Merlini and Bellotti, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on amyloid structure.

claim: Changes in stability alone cannot explain the differences in fibril formation propensity.
source: However, changes in stability alone cannot explain the differences in fibril formation propensity (Nokwe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The patient variant Pat-1 contains 11 mutations in the VL domain compared to the corresponding germline sequence WT-1.
source: The patient variant (referred to as Pat-1) contains 11 mutations in the VL domain compared to the corresponding germline sequence (referred to as WT-1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The LC variant studied was identified in a female patient who was diagnosed with a smoldering myeloma and AL amyloidosis at the age of 50 years at the Amyloidosis Center of the University of Heidelberg.
source: The LC variant studied here was identified in a female patient who was diagnosed with a smoldering myeloma and AL amyloidosis at the age of 50 years at the Amyloidosis Center of the University of Heidelberg.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient case.

claim: The LC responsible for the disease was of λ subtype.
source: The LC responsible for the disease was of λ subtype.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient case.

claim: The levels of the free λ LCs were highly elevated with 7572 mg/l in serum, compared to κ which was normal with 8 mg/l.
source: The levels of the free λ LCs were highly elevated with 7572 mg/l in serum, compared to κ which was normal with 8 mg/l.
evidence: This is clinical laboratory data from the patient case.

claim: The clonal plasma cell infiltration of the bone marrow was high reaching 80%.
source: The clonal plasma cell infiltration of the bone marrow was also high reaching 80%.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient case.

claim: Heart, kidney, lung, and soft tissue were positive for amyloid deposits and also clinically involved.
source: Heart, kidney, lung, and soft tissue were positive for amyloid deposits and also clinically involved.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient case.

claim: The cardiac stage was IV or III b indicating that the patient was suffering from advanced AL amyloidosis with poor prognosis.
source: More specifically, the cardiac stage was IV (Kumar et al., 2012) or III b (Wechalekar et al., 2013) and the renal stage was 3 (Palladini et al., 2015) indicating that the patient was suffering from advanced AL amyloidosis with poor prognosis.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient case, with staging systems referenced by citations.

claim: 4 weeks after initiation of chemotherapy, the patient died of cardiac arrest.
source: Indeed, 4 weeks after initiation of chemotherapy, the patient died of cardiac arrest.
evidence: This is clinical outcome data from the patient case.

claim: The primary structure of the pathogenic LC, named Pat-1, was deduced from the sequence of the complementary DNA (cDNA) of the plasma cell clone that caused AL amyloidosis.
source: The primary structure of the pathogenic LC, named Pat-1, was deduced from the sequence of the complementary DNA (cDNA) of the plasma cell clone that caused AL amyloidosis.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to determine the sequence.

claim: The corresponding germline LC sequence, named WT-1, was identified by database-assisted (abYsis, IgBLAST) primary structure alignments searching for the germline LC with the lowest number of residue changes with respect to the Pat-1 sequence.
source: The corresponding germline LC sequence, named WT-1, was identified by database-assisted (abYsis, IgBLAST) primary structure alignments searching for the germline LC with the lowest number of residue changes with respect to the Pat-1 sequence (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics method used to identify the germline sequence.

claim: The two sequences differ in 11 point mutations, all located in the VL domain.
source: The two sequences differ in 11 point mutations, all located in the VL domain.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Five of the mutations are located in the constant framework regions (FR) and six are in the hypervariable complementarity determining regions (CDR).
source: Five of these are located in the constant framework regions (FR) and six are in the hypervariable complementarity determining regions (CDR).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: For 9 of the 11 positions, the mutated residues in the Pat-1 VL are less abundant than the ones present in the WT-1 sequence.
source: For 9 of the 11 positions, the mutated residues in the Pat-1 VL are less abundant than the ones present in the WT-1 sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating potential negative effects on antibody structure and stability.
evidence: This is based on Kabat database frequency analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two mutated residues that show higher general frequency (S26 and D53) are located in the hypervariable CDRs.
source: The two mutated residues that show higher general frequency (S26 and D53) are located in the hypervariable CDRs.
evidence: This is based on Kabat database frequency analysis and sequence location data.

claim: Extraction of fibrils from patient abdominal fat tissue revealed that predominantly the VL domain was deposited.
source: Extraction of the fibrils followed by SDS-PAGE, MALDI fingerprint analysis of the specific band (data not shown) and its mass revealed that in this patient predominantly the VL domain was deposited (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SDS-PAGE, MALDI analysis, and mass spectrometry shown in the figures.

claim: Full length Pat-1 and WT-1 LCs did not form fibrils in ThT fluorescence assays.
source: In these assays, monitored by thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence, full length Pat-1 and WT-1 LCs did not form fibrils (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ThT fluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Incubation of the VL domain of Pat-1 revealed the presence of fibrils after a lag phase, while the WT-1 VL stayed soluble.
source: However, incubation of the VL domain of Pat-1 revealed the presence of fibrils after a lag phase, while the WT-1 VL stayed soluble.
evidence: This is supported by ThT fluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Pat-1 VL but not Pat-1 LC is the disease-relevant amyloidogenic species.
source: We thus conclude that the Pat-1 VL but not Pat-1 LC is the disease-relevant amyloidogenic species.
evidence: This conclusion is based on fibril formation assays and patient tissue analysis.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the presence of fibrils for Pat-1 VL samples, whereas no fibrils were detected in the WT-1 VL and both full length LCs samples.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed the presence of fibrils for Pat-1 VL samples, whereas no fibrils were detected in the WT-1 VL and both full length LCs samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by TEM imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The X-ray structure of Pat-1 was solved to 2.5 Å resolution.
source: To determine potential structural differences between the two VL variants Pat-1 and WT-1, the X-ray structure of both proteins were solved to 2.5 Å (Pat-1) and to 1.55 Å (WT-1) resolutions.
evidence: This is structural data obtained from X-ray crystallography.

claim: The X-ray structure of WT-1 was solved to 1.55 Å resolution.
source: To determine potential structural differences between the two VL variants Pat-1 and WT-1, the X-ray structure of both proteins were solved to 2.5 Å (Pat-1) and to 1.55 Å (WT-1) resolutions.
evidence: This is structural data obtained from X-ray crystallography.

claim: Both Pat-1 and WT-1 VL domains display highly similar structural properties despite forming crystals of different space groups.
source: Despite forming crystals of different space groups, both domains display highly similar structural properties (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both VL domains exhibit the typical Ig fold consisting of nine β-sheets forming a greek-key β−barrel topology with the three hypervariable CDR loops in spatial proximity.
source: They exhibit the typical Ig fold consisting of nine β-sheets forming a greek-key β−barrel topology with the three hypervariable CDR loops in spatial proximity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Six out of the 11 variations are found in the CDRs (T26S, S28N, V30F, G32D, E53D and S55D).
source: Six out of the 11 variations are found in the CDRs (T26S, S28N, V30F, G32D, E53D and S55D).
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Two mutations which flank the CDR3 loop are in close proximity to the VL-VH interface (Y90F and T105S), without disrupting the contact surface in comparison to WT-1.
source: Two of them which flank the CDR3 loop are in close proximity to the VL-VH interface (Y90F and T105S), without disrupting the contact surface in comparison to WT-1.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: The remaining three mutations (P15L, L81V and Q82L) are opposite to the antigen-binding site, located close to the C-terminal part of the VL domain.
source: The remaining three mutations (P15L, L81V and Q82L) are opposite to the antigen-binding site, located close to the C-terminal part of the VL domain.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: Analytical ultracentrifugation showed that the VLs studied are monomers in solution with sedimentation coefficients of approximately ~1.6 s.
source: Analytical ultracentrifugation showed that the VLs studied are monomers in solution with sedimentation coefficients of approximately ~1.6 s (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by AUC experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The melting temperatures (Tm) were determined to be 48.9°C and 57.0°C for Pat-1 and WT-1, respectively.
source: The melting temperatures (Tm) at which 50% of the protein is unfolded were determined to be 48.9°C and 57.0°C for Pat-1 and WT-1, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by far-UV CD-spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cm-value was found to be increased by 0.46 M GdmCl for WT-1 compared to Pat-1.
source: Both VL domains showed sigmoidal unfolding curves and the cm-value (the GdmCl concentrations at which 50% of the protein is unfolded) was found to be increased by 0.46 M GdmCl for WT-1 compared to Pat-1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by chemical unfolding data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The patient-derived variant is significantly less stable than the germline protein.
source: These results revealed that the patient-derived variant is significantly less stable than the germline protein.
evidence: This conclusion is based on thermal and chemical stability measurements.

claim: 10 out of the 11 Pat-1 VL point mutants either had minor effects on stability, were destabilizing, showed negative effects on thermal stability, or showed slight increases in chemical stability.
source: When we analyzed their thermal and chemical stabilities, we found that 10 out of the 11 Pat-1 VL point mutants either (i) only had minor effects on the stability (S26T, N28S and S105T), (ii) were even destabilizing the domain (L15P, F30V and D53E), (iii) showed a negative effect on thermal stability (D32G and D55S), or, iv) showed a slight increase in chemical stability (L82Q and F90Y) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by stability measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The mutation V81L resulted in a substantial shift of the Pat-1 VL towards the thermal and chemical stability of WT-1 with a TM of 54.6°C and a cM of 1.36 M.
source: In contrast, the mutation V81L resulted in a substantial shift of the Pat-1 VL towards the thermal and chemical stability of WT-1 with a TM of 54.6°C and a cM of 1.36 M (WT-1: TM = 57.0°C, cM = 1.43 M) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by stability measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: All Pat-1 point mutants except V81L formed amyloids.
source: Remarkably, when we performed fibril formation assays, we found that all Pat-1 point mutants except V81L formed amyloids (Figure 3C), suggesting that valine at position 81 is the main cause for the pathogenicity of Pat-1.
evidence: This is supported by ThT fluorescence fibril formation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Valine at position 81 is the main cause for the pathogenicity of Pat-1.
source: Remarkably, when we performed fibril formation assays, we found that all Pat-1 point mutants except V81L formed amyloids (Figure 3C), suggesting that valine at position 81 is the main cause for the pathogenicity of Pat-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the systematic mutagenesis and fibril formation data.

claim: All fibril forming variants showed an even lower halftime (t1/2) of fibril formation than Pat-1.
source: All fibril forming variants showed an even lower halftime (t1/2) of fibril formation than Pat-1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ThT fluorescence kinetics data.

claim: V81I did not exhibit a significant increase in thermal stability compared to Pat-1.
source: Intriguingly, V81I did not exhibit a significant increase in thermal stability compared to Pat-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by thermal stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: V81I readily forms fibrils unlike V81L.
source: Furthermore, we found that V81I, unlike V81L, readily forms fibrils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fibril formation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The protective effect observed for the V81L variant is highly specific to leucine.
source: Thus, we conclude that the protective effect observed for the V81L variant is highly specific to leucine.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of V81L and V81I mutants.

claim: The thermal stability of WT-1 L81V decreased by 5.5°C compared to WT-1.
source: The thermal stability of WT-1 L81V decreased by 5.5°C compared to WT-1 (Figure 3D) and the cM value for chemical unfolding, is reduced by 0.42 M GdmCl (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by thermal stability data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cM value for chemical unfolding of WT-1 L81V is reduced by 0.42 M GdmCl compared to WT-1.
source: The thermal stability of WT-1 L81V decreased by 5.5°C compared to WT-1 (Figure 3D) and the cM value for chemical unfolding, is reduced by 0.42 M GdmCl (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by chemical stability data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The introduction of valine at position 81 shifts WT-1 toward the stability of Pat-1.
source: Hence, the introduction of valine at position 81 shifts WT-1 toward the stability of Pat-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on stability measurements of WT-1 L81V.

claim: Upon incubation the WT-1 L81V mutant showed an increase of ThT fluorescence indicating fibril formation.
source: In the same line, upon incubation the WT-1 L81V mutant showed an increase of ThT fluorescence indicating fibril formation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by ThT fluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: It is possible to reconstitute the properties of the AL patient mutant by exchanging only one amino acid in the wild-type protein.
source: Together, these results show that it is possible to reconstitute the properties of the AL patient mutant by exchanging only one amino acid in the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the WT-1 L81V mutant data.

claim: V81 is in close proximity to L15 and L82 opposite of the antigen-binding site in the Pat-1 crystal structure.
source: The crystal structure of Pat-1 showed that V81 is in close proximity to L15 and L82 opposite of the antigen-binding site (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the Pat-1 crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: L15, V81, and L82 form a hydrophobic surface patch in Pat-1 which is not present in the WT-1 protein.
source: Focusing on the surface properties in this region, we found that these three amino acids form a hydrophobic surface patch which is not present in the WT-1 protein (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is based on surface property analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The combination of the substitutions at position 81 and 82 enhanced the increase in stability slightly.
source: The combination of the substitutions at position 81 and 82 enhanced the increase in stability slightly, whereas mutating leucine at position 15 to proline in combination with the other point mutations led to a decrease in stability (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by stability measurements shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Mutating leucine at position 15 to proline in combination with the other point mutations led to a decrease in stability.
source: The combination of the substitutions at position 81 and 82 enhanced the increase in stability slightly, whereas mutating leucine at position 15 to proline in combination with the other point mutations led to a decrease in stability (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by stability measurements shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The anti-amyloidogenic effect of V81L could be preserved in combination with the L82Q mutation.
source: The anti-amyloidogenic effect of V81L could be preserved in combination with the L82Q mutation.
evidence: This is supported by fibril formation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The presence of L15P in the mutants increased fibril formation.
source: The presence of L15P in the mutants increased fibril formation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fibril formation assay data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hydrophobic surface spot in Pat-1 plays a key role in pathogenesis.
source: From these results, we conclude that the hydrophobic surface spot in Pat-1 plays a key role in pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined mutational analysis of positions 15, 81, and 82.

claim: Pat-1 exhibits higher conformational dynamics as indicated by an overall higher HD/X rate.
source: Our analysis indicates that Pat-1 exhibits higher conformational dynamics as indicated by an overall higher HD/X rate (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by H/DX-MS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The most affected segment in H/DX-MS was the C-terminal framework region 4 (FR4, residues 101–113).
source: The most affected segment was the C-terminal framework region 4 (FR4, residues 101–113).
evidence: This is based on H/DX-MS data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The region from amino acid 11 to 20 (FR1), comprising the residue at position 15, shows increased fractional uptake of deuterium in Pat-1.
source: Additionally, the region from amino acid 11 to 20 (FR1), comprising the residue at position 15 which is part of the surface-exposed hydrophobic spot, is striking since the fractional uptake of deuterium in Pat-1 increases in this area.
evidence: This is based on H/DX-MS data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Pat-1 VL shows a higher flexibility in most parts of the domain compared to WT-1.
source: When the differences in fractional deuterium uptake between Pat-1 and WT-1 are mapped onto the X-ray structure of Pat-1, it becomes obvious that the Pat-1 VL shows a higher flexibility in most parts of the domain compared to WT-1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on H/DX-MS data mapped onto the crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The mutations at position 15, 81 and 82 result in a change in hydrophobic interactions between Pat-1 and WT-1.
source: To determine the underlying molecular reasons for the differences in dynamics and stability, we analyzed side chain interactions in the structures of the VL domains using the BIOVA Discovery Studio software. We found that the mutations at position 15, 81 and 82 result in a change in hydrophobic interactions between Pat-1 and WT-1 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the crystal structures shown in Figure 6.

claim: In WT-1, P15 is not involved in a hydrophobic interaction network.
source: In WT-1, this proline is not involved in a hydrophobic interaction network.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of hydrophobic interactions.

claim: In the patient mutant L15 interacts with three amino acids located in FR3, including the two other point mutations in the hydrophobic surface spot, and two residues in the C-terminal region (V111 and L112).
source: In contrast, in the patient mutant L15 interacts with three amino acids located in FR3, including the two other point mutations in the hydrophobic surface spot, and two residues in the C-terminal region (V111 and L112).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of hydrophobic interactions shown in Figure 6.

claim: The contact of L15 to the very dynamic C-terminal segment induces the enhanced conformational dynamics of the respective loop region in FR1.
source: Thus, the contact of L15 to the very dynamic C-terminal segment, as indicated by the HD/X rate, induces the enhanced conformational dynamics of the respective loop region in FR1.
evidence: This is an inference based on H/DX-MS data and structural analysis.

claim: V81 in Pat-1 forms six hydrophobic interactions with residues in FR2 and FR3, two of them with L15 and L82.
source: V81 in Pat-1 forms six hydrophobic interactions with residues in FR2 and FR3, two of them, the L15 and L82 point mutations, are located within this hydrophobic surface area.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of hydrophobic interactions shown in Figure 6.

claim: V81 contacts only one amino acid in the C-terminal segment (V111).
source: However, V81 contacts only one amino acid in the C-terminal segment (V111).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of hydrophobic interactions shown in Figure 6.

claim: L81 in WT-1 forms three hydrophobic interactions to the C-terminal region (V109, V111 and L112).
source: The hydrophobic interaction pattern of the WT-1 L81 misses one interaction each in FR2 and in FR3 but two more interactions to the C-terminal region appear. Overall, this leads to three hydrophobic interactions of L81 to the C-terminal region (V109, V111 and L112).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of hydrophobic interactions shown in Figure 6.

claim: L82 can form five hydrophobic interactions with FR2-4.
source: For the mutation at position 82, the biggest effect comes from the change of the nature of interaction from hydrophobic to hydrophilic and the resulting decrease of hydrophobic surface area. L82 can form five hydrophobic interactions with FR2-4.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of interactions.

claim: Q82 forms hydrophilic interactions to four residues, all located in FR3: R64, E84, D85 and E86.
source: Q82 however forms hydrophilic interactions to four residues, all located in FR3: R64, E84, D85 and E86.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of interactions.

claim: The network of interactions in the C-terminal region is markedly changed in Pat-1 by the mutations at position 15, 81 and 82 leading to a highly dynamic C-terminal region.
source: We conclude that the network of interactions in the C-terminal region is markedly changed in Pat-1 by the mutations at position 15, 81 and 82 leading to a highly dynamic C-terminal region.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis and H/DX-MS data.

claim: The free energy simulations exhibit similar dissociation free energies for the WT-1 and the single back mutation V81L, which were higher (by ~1 kcal·mol−1) in comparison to Pat-1 and the double back mutation V81L L15P.
source: The free energy simulations exhibit similar dissociation free energies for the WT-1 and the single back mutation V81L, which were higher (by ~1 kcal·mol−1) in comparison to Pat-1 and the double back mutation V81L L15P.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics umbrella sampling simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: The increased dissociation free energy indicates an increased protein stability for WT-1 and the back mutation of Pat-1 V81L.
source: This indicates an increased protein stability for WT-1 and the back mutation of Pat-1 V81L.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the molecular dynamics simulation results.

claim: The effect of the V81L mutation is mainly due to a small cavity that is present in the case of V81 and that is filled if V81 is replaced by a slightly larger residue (V81L).
source: The effect of the V81L mutation is mainly due to a small cavity that is present in the case of V81 and that is filled if V81 is replaced by a slightly larger residue (V81L) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: The double back mutation V81L L15P exhibited a significant reduction of the dissociation free energy (by ~1 kcal·mol−1) relative to the patient mutant.
source: However, a destabilizing effect due to the additional back mutation L15P could be observed. Here, the double back mutation exhibited an opposite effect compared to the single back mutation, by producing a significant reduction of the dissociation free energy (by ~1 kcal·mol−1) relative to the patient mutant.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics umbrella sampling simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: The destabilizing effect of L15P can be explained by a change in the local protein backbone structure that changes the local packing geometry and offsets the effect of the V81L mutation.
source: This effect can be explained by a change in the local protein backbone structure (due to the L15P) that changes the local packing geometry and offsets the effect of the V81L mutation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the molecular dynamics simulation results.

claim: For Pat-1, the full length LC is resistant to fibril formation.
source: For Pat-1, the full length LC is resistant to fibril formation.
evidence: This is based on ThT fluorescence fibril formation assays.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage in the linker region between the VL and CL domain is a prerequisite to unleash the amyloidogenic potential of the mutations in VL.
source: Proteolytic cleavage in the linker region between the VL and CL domain is a prerequisite to unleash the amyloidogenic potential of the mutations in VL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on fibril formation assays comparing full-length LC and VL domains.

claim: Recent cryo-EM structures of AL fibrils showed a highly diffuse density for the C-terminal residues of the VL domain indicating a flexible orientation.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures of AL fibrils showed a highly diffuse density for the C-terminal residues of the VL domain indicating a flexible orientation. Thus, the exact pathogenic truncation site between VL and CL does not seem to be crucial (Radamaker et al., 2019; Swuec et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: The exact pathogenic truncation site between VL and CL does not seem to be crucial.
source: Recent cryo-EM structures of AL fibrils showed a highly diffuse density for the C-terminal residues of the VL domain indicating a flexible orientation. Thus, the exact pathogenic truncation site between VL and CL does not seem to be crucial (Radamaker et al., 2019; Swuec et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited cryo-EM structural studies.

claim: NMR studies suggest the existence of different fibril topologies in VL amyloid fibrils.
source: NMR studies further suggest the existence of different fibril topologies in VL amyloid fibrils. They may contain well-ordered and rigid C-terminal ends or a highly ordered hydrophobic core domain (Hora et al., 2017; Piehl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to NMR studies.

claim: Small amounts of SDS presented during incubation accelerate the fibril formation process.
source: It was shown earlier that small amounts of SDS presented during the incubation accelerate the process (Kihara et al., 2005; Nokwe et al., 2015; Yamamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SDS in concentrations used in this study do not affect the native secondary structure.
source: In this study, we use SDS in concentrations that do not affect the native secondary structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by far-UV CD spectra shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deposits from abdominal fat tissue were previously shown to be identical to organ-specific fibrils.
source: These deposits were previously shown to be identical to organ-specific fibrils (Annamalai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The fibril load in organs correlates to the severity of the disease in AL patients.
source: As the fibril load in organs correlates to the severity of the disease in AL patients, we studied fibril formation in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The current view holds that the overall destabilization of the VL domain is a major indicator for fibril formation propensity.
source: The current view holds that the overall destabilization of the VL domain is a major indicator for fibril formation propensity (Blancas-Mejía et al., 2015; Morgan and Kelly, 2016; Nokwe et al., 2014; Ramirez-Alvarado, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VL domains with wildtype-like stability were found to form fibrils.
source: Furthermore, also VL domains with wildtype-like stability were found to form fibrils (Nokwe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Surface-exposed hydrophobic areas are known to be energetically unfavorable.
source: Since surface-exposed hydrophobic areas are known to be energetically unfavorable (Eisenhaber and Argos, 1996; Moelbert et al., 2004; Young et al., 1994), we investigated these amino acids regarding their stability and amyloidogenic properties.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on protein energetics.

claim: The single L82Q substitution did not affect the stability of Pat-1 and the mutant still formed fibrils.
source: Against our expectations, the single L82Q substitution did not affect the stability of Pat-1 and the mutant still formed fibrils.
evidence: This is based on stability measurements and fibril formation assays.

claim: Oligomers formed on the pathway to highly organized amyloid structures are considered toxic.
source: In general, there are different hypotheses on the nature of the toxic species in amyloid diseases. Besides fibrils, Oligomers formed on the pathway to highly organized amyloid structures are considered toxic (Merlini, 2017; Riek and Eisenberg, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on amyloid toxicity.

claim: Amyloid deposits consist not only of the disease-causing LC but also contain many other factors like glycosaminoglycans, lipids, apolipoprotein E or other proteins.
source: Furthermore, it is well-known that amyloid deposits consist not only of the disease-causing LC but also contain many other factors like glycosaminoglycans, lipids, apolipoprotein E or other proteins.
evidence: This is stated as well-known knowledge in the field.

claim: Many factors in amyloid deposits have been shown to influence fibril formation in the context of amyloid diseases.
source: Many of these factors have already been shown to influence fibril formation in the context of amyloid diseases (Gellermann et al., 2005; Wyatt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
